body: Holding a plastic cup of something she has not drunk, a woman of about forty is sitting in a hospital corridor at twenty past three in the morning. Across from her a family she has never met are asleep along four chairs, one of them with a coat over his head. A cleaner comes past with a machine and does not look up. There is nothing to do, nothing to decide and nobody to telephone, because everyone she would ring is asleep and would have to be woken for it. She waits. Somewhere down the ward a lift arrives and nobody gets out of it.

Nothing was happening in that corridor, and that is the difficulty rather than the relief. The hours after midnight are not busy hours. They are empty ones, and an empty hour with something heavy sitting in it is the longest unit of time there is.

Radio schedules are built around the waking day. Breakfast, drive, afternoon, evening — the hours advertisers pay for, and the hours most people are in fact awake. What sits between midnight and five is almost always automation, because nobody is buying it.

It is worth taking the word midnight literally, because Scripture does. The night in the ancient world was not one block of undifferentiated dark; it was divided into watches, and a watch was a shift that somebody actually stood, awake on purpose while the town slept. That is the frame the text keeps returning to. The psalmist calls to remembrance his song in the night. Job asks after the God who gives songs in the night. The writer of the longest psalm rises at midnight to give thanks, and what gets written down is the hour rather than the sentiment. The dark is treated as an occasion in its own right rather than as dead ground between two days.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations. One of them is programmed for these hours specifically, and its bases sit in Dublin, Chicago and Seattle — eight hours apart end to end, so that midnight rolls rather than arriving everywhere at once.

That is the least commercially defensible frequency on the band and one of the easiest to justify. Nobody buys these hours. There is no breakfast sponsor at four in the morning and no drive-time at half past two, and a station that programmes them properly is spending real money on the smallest audience it will ever have. It is spent anyway, and the reason is in the text rather than in the strategy. Paul and Silas sang at midnight. The hour is recorded, and Scripture does not usually waste words on the time.

The hours have not been left empty, though. They have been colonised by everything that does best when a person is tired and on their own. The feed that does not end. The autoplay that starts the next thing before the last has finished. The betting advert that runs at three because at three it works. None of that is a conspiracy; it is simply where the returns are. Attention is cheapest at night and judgement is weakest, and an industry that buys the first and lives off the second will always find the hour worth having. What it has never once done is keep anybody company.

The station is built the other way about. It is ambient worship — Celtic and European, contemplative, largely instrumental, with a good deal of space left between things, because a track that arrives every ninety seconds is a demand and not a comfort. The schedule names the hours for what they are: The Long Night from ten, and at three in the morning the Watch of the Fourth Hour. That is the whole register. It assumes you are awake for a reason and does not ask what the reason is.
None of which is background music, and none of it is a sleep aid. The difference matters here, because the difference is the argument.

Be fair to the sleep app first, because it does something real. Rain on a roof, a low drone, a voice pitched deliberately flat — these lower a heart rate, and for somebody who cannot get under they are worth the money. But notice what they are for. They are engineered to make you unconscious, addressed to your body, with nothing whatever to say to the thing that woke you. When the technique fails, and at three it often does, you are left in a room with a sound in it, which is not the same as being left in a room with somebody in it.
The night does not need soothing. What it lacks is company.

A man of fifty-two has been waking at twenty to four every night since the redundancy, and he has stopped fighting it. He goes down. He does not put the big light on, because the big light makes it a proper night rather than a bad patch of one. His wife will be up at half six and he will tell her he slept all right. Some weeks ago he started putting the radio on quietly at the counter, on the one frequency doing anything at that hour, and he leaves it until the sky over the fence starts to go the colour it goes. He has not told anybody that he does this. He is not praying, exactly. He is simply not on his own in the kitchen.
Nothing in that was a decision he would call religious, and nothing was asked of him. Somebody was awake and audible at the hour he happened to be awake, and that is the whole of the mechanism.

This has a limit, and it should be said plainly. A frequency is not a person. There is nobody on the other end of it at four in the morning who knows your name or will ring you back, and no arrangement of music makes the thing that woke you any less true. It will not find him work, it will not undo a diagnosis, and it will not make the corridor shorter. There are nights when a station is not remotely enough, and pretending otherwise would be a cheap thing to do on this subject.

But the singing in that prison did not open the doors either. An earthquake did that, and it came afterwards. What the account bothers to record is that the other prisoners heard them — men who had not asked for it, in the dark, with their own reasons for being awake. That is what praise at midnight has always been. Not a technique for changing the hour, but a refusal to let the hour have the last word in it, carried out loud, where somebody else can hear that it is being done at all.

So programming the empty hours is neither sentimental nor charitable. These are the hours in which people are least able to manage themselves and least able to ask, and a broadcast band does not require them to ask. Grief arrives at three. So does the worry that will not settle, the sick child, the shift that ends when everybody else is asleep. Something already running is the only thing that reaches a person who is not going to reach out.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. At three in the morning any of them will play. One of them was designed for three in the morning.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 314.40 — Midnight Praise. It is the frequency this article has been describing: ambient worship, Celtic and European, contemplative rather than energetic, with the space left in that most stations hurry to fill. Its named hours are The Long Night at ten and the Watch of the Fourth Hour at three, which tells you what it thinks it is doing. Put it on low in a kitchen, or on a ward corridor with one earphone in, and let it run. It will not ask you anything. It will not brighten up at five to reassure you. It keeps the watch alongside you, which is the one thing that hour has never been offered by anybody with something to sell.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are reaching for and at what hours — which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. You do not have to believe a word about the fourth watch to test it, and you certainly do not have to be at your best. The next time you are awake at an hour you did not choose, put HM 314.40 on quietly and go back to whatever you were not managing to do. Somebody arranged those hours on the assumption that you would be there. Let them turn out to have been right.
